Note · Kahneman, Sibony & Sunstein — Noise

4 min read846 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-kahneman-sibony-sunstein-noise.md

Canon · Cluster: Behavioral Design & Decision Science · Maps to Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making), E6 (Crisis Leadership)

  • Source: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (2021)
  • Core claim: Bias's overlooked twin is noise. Bias is systematic error (everyone skews the same way); noise is random scatter (different people — or the same person on different days — reach wildly different conclusions from identical facts). Orgs obsess over bias and almost never measure noise, though noise may do more damage.
  • Framework:
  • Total error² = bias² + noise² — they add; reducing only bias leaves half the problem.
  • Evidence: judges give very different sentences for identical cases; underwriters quote very different premiums for the same risk; doctors diagnose the same symptoms differently.
  • Decision hygiene to cut noise: gather independent judgments before discussion (avoid anchoring/cascades), use shared scales / reference classes, aggregate multiple assessments, structure judgments into independent components, and favor rules/algorithms for repeated judgments.
  • Applies when: any organization makes repeated professional judgments — hiring, pricing, grading, underwriting, performance review — where consistency itself has value.
  • Breaks when: noise reduction can over-rotate into rigid algorithmization that strips legitimate, expert, case-sensitive discretion (Klein's recognition-primed expertise is not noise, canon klein sources of power — telling them apart is hard). "Independent judgments first" is procedurally costly and culturally resisted. And some variance is signal, not noise — flattening it can erase real differences.

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — book-specific Noise summary transcript, "Noise by Daniel Kahneman: Animated Book Summary," youtube.com/watch?v=KntsGhV3rvM) The actionable kernel is the book's own archer image: a team all "missing low and to the left" is biased but coachable; a team "missing the bullseye all over the target" is noisy — and "a team that is noisily missing is much harder to coach than a team that is missing due to bias" (KntsGhV3rvM). That is exactly why noise is the neglected problem: bias is "easy to identify," a noisy process "is much harder to identify and fix." The practitioner translation is concrete and uncomfortable — "it is likely that an assessment would depend more on the person doing the review than the performance of the person being judged" (KntsGhV3rvM). So in hiring/review, score independently before the meeting: the same transcript warns that "who speaks first or last, who speaks with the most confidence, who is smiling" contaminates group judgment. Pairs with Tetlock's calibration (canon tetlock superforecasting).

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): The book splits error into two species. "Some judgments are biased — they are systematically off target. Other judgments are noisy, as people who are expected to agree end up at very different points around the target" (Kahneman, quoted in "Noise by Daniel Kahneman: Animated Book Summary," KntsGhV3rvM). The wedge is the word judgment itself: unlike an opinion or taste, "the word judgment implies that everyone should agree and come to the same conclusion… we expect judgments to be agreed upon" (KntsGhV3rvM) — and they don't. A second book summary nails the operative definition: noise is "the random variation in judgments that should be consistent when evaluating the same information… the background static that can disrupt the decision-making process" ("Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Book Summary)," 0qVNXLZygDs). Hence Total error² = bias² + noise²: kill bias and you still leave the scatter.
  • Real application (mined): the transcript lists the book's own six fixes, which read as a field checklist: "accept that decisions are about accuracy and not individual expression… think statistically and take an outside view… structure judgment into independent tasks… take independent judgments from multiple judges and average them out… and favor relative judgments, which tend to be less noisy" (KntsGhV3rvM). The second summary frames the same as decision hygiene — "using checklists, algorithms and standardized criteria" and "establishing clear decision criteria, providing feedback and promoting a culture of accountability" (0qVNXLZygDs). The canonical examples to audit first: "the variability in legal sentencing where identical cases can result in different sentences depending on the judge," and "medical diagnosis can vary widely among doctors" (0qVNXLZygDs).
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the same transcript that sells the fix also flags its limit — "algorithms are not immune to biases" (0qVNXLZygDs). The book's preferred remedy (rules/algorithms for repeated judgments) trades scatter for whatever the rule bakes in, so aggressive algorithmization can flatten legitimate, case-sensitive expertise — Klein's recognition-primed variance is signal, not noise, and telling the two apart is the unsolved hard problem (canon klein sources of power).
  • Sources in corpus: "Noise by Daniel Kahneman: Animated Book Summary" (youtube.com/watch?v=KntsGhV3rvM) · "Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Book Summary)" (youtube.com/watch?v=0qVNXLZygDs). (r/decisionmaking pull returned empty — no Reddit sources cited.)

Rep

Run a noise audit on one repeated decision: have 3 people independently score the same case without conferring. The spread is your noise. Then add one hygiene step (independent-first) and re-measure.
